slides.headline: The summary
slides.body: Four parts, in this order, fitting on one screen.

rows: 1. What happened
What was affected, for how long, with what impact
Impact first, in business terms. Times with a time zone. No names
2. Root cause
Which mechanism, on which layer
One sentence, with the layer named: a Git default, a GitHub rule that was missing, a GitHub Actions default
3. What was done, and how it was verified
Is it over
The recovery in one sentence, and the check that proves it. State what is not yet verified
4. Prevention
Will it recur
The control, its owner, its date. A control, not a promise to be careful

slides.headline: Five habits make a summary trustworthy
slides.body: Separate what you observed from what you infer, and say which is which.

slides.headline: Five habits make a summary trustworthy

slides.headline: When not to use any of this
slides.body: Don't run an incident process for a SEV 4, the lowest level.
Three pictures help. For the summary, think of a pilot's announcement after turbulence.
Where the picture breaks: passengers can't act on what they hear.
For blamelessness, think of the next incident.
For controls, the ranking is a ladder again, and this time you climb as high as you can.

slides.direction: The summary form of section 30.15, written for the rewritten production branch. Show it as a slide and read it part by part.
slides.text:
Subject: [Resolved] billing-api: production branch history rewritten (SEV 2, no customer impact)

What happened   Between <time> and <time> IST the branch "production" of billing-api pointed at a rewritten
                history. Nothing was deployed from it: the release job refused. A staging build from that
                branch showed unrounded tax amounts.
Root cause      A history clean-up (interactive rebase) on "production" was force-pushed. It replaced four
                commits by one and dropped the tax-rounding fix. Git allows this; our GitHub rules for the
                branch did not block force pushes.
What was done   The recorded history was restored from the deployment tag and the one change shipped in
                between was carried over. Verified: the deployed commit is again an ancestor of the branch
                (the release job's own check), and the rounding fix is in the file. All three known clones
                were realigned. Not yet verified: clones on CI caches; they are rebuilt tonight.
Prevention      A ruleset on "production" (no force pushes, no deletions, pull request required, no bypass).
                Owner: platform team. Active since <time> today.

slides.direction: The postmortem template of section 30.19, as a second slide.
slides.text:
# Postmortem: <one-line title>            Severity: SEV n        Status: draft | reviewed | actions closed

## Summary             Four sentences: what happened, root cause with its layer, what was done, what prevents it.
## Impact              Who and what was affected, for how long. What could have happened in the window.
## Timeline            Time (with zone) | event | source of the fact (reflog entry, tag, log line, message)
## Detection           How it was noticed, by whom or what, and how long after it began.
## Root cause          The seven-line root-cause box of Chapter 1, section 1.10.
## Contributing conditions   What made the action look right. Which control was missing or bypassed.
## Recovery            What was done, in order, with risk labels. What was verified, and how.
## What went well      The controls and habits that limited the damage.
## What went badly     Without names.
## Actions             Control | type (prevent, detect, recover) | owner | date | how we will know it works
## Evidence            Transcripts, commit IDs, links. Kept with the document.

slides.body: Now the four questions, against this timeline.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Answering the CTO with commands. Root cause: the summary is written from the engineer's experience of the incident instead of from the three decisions its reader has to make.
Writing "verified" for something that was inferred. Root cause: the check was not run, and the claim was made to make the incident sound closed.
A timeline without sources. Root cause: times were taken from memory or chat, so they cannot be reconciled when two accounts differ.

A postmortem that names a person as the cause. Root cause: it explains who acted instead of why the action looked right and why nothing stopped it, so it changes nothing in the system and teaches people to hide evidence.
"We will be more careful" as the action. Root cause: no layer was identified that could have refused the action, so there is nothing that still works when someone is new, tired or in a hurry.

beats.text: From root cause to control. A control is something that still works when the person is new, tired or in a hurry. Controls differ in strength, and the order of the table is the order in which to look for one.

beats.text: Four questions take you from root cause to control. Which layer could have refused the action: the platform, the pipeline, the client, a reviewer? What is the strongest control available on that layer and on your plan, since some ruleset features are plan-gated? What will the control block that is legitimate, and what is the path for that case? And how will you know it works: a ruleset's insights, a test that fails when the fix is removed, an attempt in a sandbox.

And how will you know it works: a ruleset's insights, a test that fails when the fix is removed, an attempt in a sandbox.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A release job tests the ancestry of a branch and refuses to deploy a rewritten one. Is that control A, prevent, B, detect, or C, recover? Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. A release job tests the ancestry of a branch and refuses to deploy a rewritten one. Is that control A, prevent, B, detect, or C, recover? Your answer?

beats.text: Prevent, detect, recover. The answer is B. The template's action table asks for the type of each control. A ruleset, GitHub's named list of rules for chosen branches, that refuses a forced push prevents. The release job's ancestry test detects: the rewrite had already happened, and the job noticed before deployment.
beats.tele: Prevent, detect, recover. The answer is B. The template's action table asks for the type of each control. A ruleset, GitHub's named list of rules for chosen branches, that refuses a forced push prevents. The release job's ancestry test detects: the rewrite had already happened, and the job noticed before deployment.

beats.text: A backup ref, a deployment tag that names the running commit, or a clone that hasn't fetched is what lets you recover. A good set of actions has at least a prevent and a detect, because every prevention has a bypass.
beats.tele: A backup ref, a deployment tag that names the running commit, or a clone that hasn't fetched is what lets you recover. A good set of actions has at least a prevent and a detect, because every prevention has a bypass.

beats.text: Prefer one strong control to five weak ones. For the rewritten production branch the list could have ten items. The one that matters is a checkbox on the server. "Engineers will take more care" is not a control.
beats.tele: Prefer one strong control to five weak ones. For the rewritten production branch the list could have ten items. The one that matters is a checkbox on the server. "Engineers will take more care" is not a control.

beats.text: When not to use any of this. Don't run an incident process for a SEV 4, the lowest level. One person's local reset needs ten minutes of help and one note, not a channel and a document.
beats.tele: When not to use any of this. Don't run an incident process for a SEV 4, the lowest level. One person's local reset needs ten minutes of help and one note, not a channel and a document.

beats.text: Three pictures help. For the summary, think of a pilot's announcement after turbulence. It has four sentences: what happened, why, that the aircraft is fine and how the crew knows, and what will be done differently for the rest of the flight. Nobody in the cabin wants the control inputs. And a pilot who says "everything is checked" before the check is done has spent the passengers' trust for the rest of the flight.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: passengers can't act on what they hear. A CTO can and will. The fourth sentence is a request for a decision, with an owner and a date in it.
beats.tele: Where the picture breaks: passengers can't act on what they hear. A CTO can and will. The fourth sentence is a request for a decision, with an owner and a date in it.

beats.text: For blamelessness, think of the next incident. The person who caused this one holds the evidence for it, and will be near the next one too. Whatever happens to them now decides whether the next reflog is pasted into the channel or quietly collected.
beats.tele: For blamelessness, think of the next incident. The person who caused this one holds the evidence for it, and will be near the next one too. Whatever happens to them now decides whether the next reflog is pasted into the channel or quietly collected.

beats.text: For controls, the ranking is a ladder again, and this time you climb as high as you can. The ladder of video 184 said: take the lowest rung that repairs. This one says: take the highest rung that prevents.
beats.tele: For controls, the ranking is a ladder again, and this time you climb as high as you can. The ladder of video 184 said: take the lowest rung that repairs. This one says: take the highest rung that prevents.

beats.text: Point at four things. The subject line carries status, severity and impact. The root cause names both layers: "Git allows this; our GitHub rules did not block it". The third part has the words "Not yet verified". And there is no name anywhere.

beats.text: Three lines carry most of the weight. The timeline has a third column: the source of the fact. "Contributing conditions" is where blamelessness is done: what made the action look right. And the last column of "Actions": how we will know it works.

beats.text: The deployment. When was the running commit deployed, and which commit is it?
beats.tele: The deployment. When was the running commit deployed, and which commit is it?

beats.text: Timeline line one: 10:14, plus 05:30, the release job tagged 3277739 as deployed. Source: the annotated tag, a named pointer to a commit that records who tagged it and when, with its tagger date and its message. The tag is a witness that no later rewrite could alter.

beats.text: The rewrite. When was the branch rewritten, and when was the rewrite published? Predict which clone's reflogs can answer. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: The rewrite. When was the branch rewritten, and when was the rewrite published? Predict which clone's reflogs can answer. Say it out loud.

beats.text: The clone that did the rewriting. Two more lines. 10:25: a rebase of production finished in one clone. 10:26: the result was amended. Source: that clone's branch reflog. 10:27: the rewritten branch was pushed. Source: that clone's reflog of the remote-tracking branch, "update by push". In the document these lines say "a rebase finished in a developer's clone", not a name.

beats.text: The adoption. When did a second clone adopt the rewrite, and when did new work land on it?
beats.tele: The adoption. When did a second clone adopt the rewrite, and when did new work land on it?

beats.text: 10:28: a second clone fetched and saw a forced update. 10:29: its branch was reset to the server's. 10:30: a new commit was made on top. 10:31: that commit was pushed. Four lines, four sources, from two reflogs of the second clone.

beats.text: The detection.
beats.tele: The detection.

beats.text: 10:33: our own clone first saw the forced update. In real life the detection line is the time of the alert: here, the release job's refusal.

beats.text: Now read the timeline as the postmortem would. How long was it from the publication of the rewrite to our detection? Work it out, and say it out loud.
beats.tele: Now read the timeline as the postmortem would. How long was it from the publication of the rewrite to our detection? Work it out, and say it out loud.

beats.text: Six minutes. From 10:27 to the restore, the server's branch pointed at a rewritten history: that's the window of the summary's first part. Between the publication at 10:27 and the detection, six minutes passed, and in those six minutes a second clone adopted the rewrite and shipped on top of it. That interval is the "Detection" section, and it's the argument for the control: the earlier the server refuses, the shorter this list.

beats.text: Notice what the sandbox let us do that real life doesn't. We read two colleagues' reflogs directly. In real life you ask a colleague to run git reflog show --date=iso origin/production and paste it. Whether they do depends on what happened to the last person who pasted one.

beats.text: Now the four questions, against this timeline. The layer that could have refused is the platform: the push at 10:27 was a forced update of a production branch. The strongest control there is a ruleset that blocks force pushes, with an empty bypass list. Its type is prevent. And the detect control already exists and worked: the release job's ancestry test.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Answering the CTO with commands. Root cause: the summary is written from the engineer's experience of the incident instead of from the three decisions its reader has to make.
beats.tele: Answering the CTO with commands. Root cause: the summary is written from the engineer's experience of the incident instead of from the three decisions its reader has to make.

beats.text: Writing "verified" for something that was inferred. Root cause: the check was not run, and the claim was made to make the incident sound closed.
beats.tele: Writing "verified" for something that was inferred. Root cause: the check was not run, and the claim was made to make the incident sound closed.

beats.text: A timeline without sources. Root cause: times were taken from memory or chat, so they cannot be reconciled when two accounts differ.
beats.tele: A timeline without sources. Root cause: times were taken from memory or chat, so they cannot be reconciled when two accounts differ.

beats.text: A postmortem that names a person as the cause. Root cause: it explains who acted instead of why the action looked right and why nothing stopped it, so it changes nothing in the system and teaches people to hide evidence.
beats.tele: A postmortem that names a person as the cause. Root cause: it explains who acted instead of why the action looked right and why nothing stopped it, so it changes nothing in the system and teaches people to hide evidence.

beats.text: "We will be more careful" as the action. Root cause: no layer was identified that could have refused the action, so there is nothing that still works when someone is new, tired or in a hurry.
beats.tele: "We will be more careful" as the action. Root cause: no layer was identified that could have refused the action, so there is nothing that still works when someone is new, tired or in a hurry.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. After the rewritten production branch of a billing service has been restored, the engineer who led the recovery writes the summary before she goes home. It's the slide you saw: four parts, one screen, with one sentence that says what is not yet verified, the CI caches, and when it will be.

beats.text: The postmortem follows within three days. She builds the timeline from two colleagues' reflogs, which they paste without hesitation, because the first sentence she said to them on the day was "nobody is in trouble; I need your reflogs before you fetch again". Under "Contributing conditions" she writes what made the clean-up look right: the branch had accumulated fixup commits, the developer had been told to keep history tidy, and nothing distinguished production from any other branch at the moment of the push.

beats.text: Under "What went well": an ancestry check in the release job that somebody added two years earlier.
beats.tele: Under "What went well": an ancestry check in the release job that somebody added two years earlier.

beats.text: The action table has two rows. A ruleset on production, type prevent, owner the platform team, active the same day, verified by an attempted forced push in a test repository with the same ruleset. And an alert on the release job's refusal, type detect, so that the next refusal reaches a person in minutes. She resists adding eight more rows.

beats.text: Before you run a command, list the events you expect the timeline to contain and, for each, predict which repository's reflog or which tag will be its source. Then build the timeline with a source on every line. Write the four-part summary on one screen, mark each statement in the third part as observed or inferred, and include one sentence that begins "Not yet verified". Then say the four parts aloud, one sentence each, in under a minute.

beats.text: The challenge is Lab 38.2, "A blameless postmortem", in the same file. Apply the test: replace every name by a role and read it again.

beats.text: Read the question, then answer out loud, in under two minutes.
beats.tele: Read the question, then answer out loud, in under two minutes.

beats.text: A strong answer gives the four parts in order and, for each, the question it answers for the reader, not only its title. It gives the rules that make each part usable: impact first and in business terms, the layer named in the root cause, an owner and a date in the prevention.

beats.text: For the third part it states the rule and its positive counterpart: what you do write when a check hasn't been run yet. If you add when the first version of a summary is sent, and why, you've shown that you understand it as a tool during the incident and not as paperwork after it.

beats.text: Let's land this.
beats.tele: Let's land this.

beats.text: The summary has four parts: what happened, the root cause with its layer, what was done and how it was verified, and what prevents a repeat.
beats.tele: The summary has four parts: what happened, the root cause with its layer, what was done and how it was verified, and what prevents a repeat.

beats.text: Never write "verified" for a check that was not run, and always state what is not yet verified.
beats.tele: Never write "verified" for a check that was not run, and always state what is not yet verified.

beats.text: Every line of a timeline carries its source: a reflog entry, a tag, a log line, a message.
beats.tele: Every line of a timeline carries its source: a reflog entry, a tag, a log line, a message.

beats.text: A postmortem is blameless so that it explains the system and so that people keep handing over evidence; replace names by roles to test it.
beats.tele: A postmortem is blameless so that it explains the system and so that people keep handing over evidence; replace names by roles to test it.

beats.text: A control is ranked by what enforces it, from "the server refuses" down to habit, and it comes with an owner, a date and a way to know that it works.
